Mr Speaker, some have expressed the opinion in this house that we should not avail ourselves of the opportunity of expressing our congratulations to those who have performed services and attained an office of prominence. I am not one of those who subscribe to such views. I think that this debate permits each one of us, as members of this house, to express our thanks for work well done and also to express our congratulations on the services performed on our behalf in the past and on the positions attained today. Therefore, Mr. Speaker, may I congratulate you on your elevation to the position you now hold. It is the result of conscientious hard work on behalf of the members of this house over a period of time. With your courtesy, geniality and fairmindedness I am sure that we in this house will have reason to be extremely proud of the position which you hold and you will, I am sure, lend dignity to all of us. As an English-speaking member from the province of Ontario, I think we are doubly proud of the fact that you, representing a Frenchspeaking seat in the province of Quebec, have been elected to this high office. We in Ontario are also proud and most favoured in having the Deputy Speaker appointed from our province by the members of this house. We know that he will give you support. He too will lend dignity and grace to the debates.
I too, Mr. Speaker, should like to extend my congratulations to the mover (Mr. Hol-lingworth) and the seconder (Mr. Villeneuve) of the address in reply to the speech from the throne. I am not so well acquainted with the seconder, but from what he has done in this house and the way he has conducted himself I am sure that we shall be hearing a great deal from him and that we shall be proud of the work which he will accomplish in the term now commencing.
The mover is better known to me, and I am sure he is well known to all members of the house. Over a period of years he has performed many services on behalf not only of the people of his own constituency but of all the people of Canada, a fact which is greatly appreciated. He has recently been elected. He fought a good, clean, hard fight.

It is interesting to note that his chief opponent, who was a man of great influence and, I think, probably of great wealth, has now sought refuge in the old country following the example of one of his predecessors. I think it is only fitting that I recommend to the mother country that suitable rewards should be given to him for the service which he has accomplished in Canada in acquiring a great chain of newspapers and in serving the people of our country.
The people whom I represent in the constituency of Essex West are. for the most part, engaged in the automobile industry. We have, of course, the largest concentration of the pharmaceutical industry in the British Empire; but in addition to that we are known as the centre of the automobile industry in the British Empire. We have a large plant of the General Motors Corporation which manufactures the motors used in trucks and motor cars. Then too we have a large plant of the Ford Motor Company which recently has expended about $7 million or $8 million on the expansion of a power plant and which now has embarked on a program of expansion of their plant there to the extent of some several millions of dollars. I am not certain as to the amount but I think it is in the neighbourhood of about $20 million. The third large corporation which we have is the Chrysler Corporation of Canada. They have never been known as any particular supporters of mine, I might tell you; but they have shown their faith in this country of ours and their hopes for the future by embarking on a program under which they will, in the next eighteen months or so, expend approximately $41 million in enlarging considerably the plants they now have.
On looking back over the years, Mr. Speaker-if I may be facetious for a moment-we recall that the automobile industry started here in Canada about 50 years ago. They are making quite a few sales. There are quite a few automobiles in the hands of our people-whether that is good or bad-and we are all endeavouring to get possession of one if we do not already have one. As I say, if I may be facetious, I have been coming to the conclusion that the automobile is really here to stay.
In its plant the Chrysler corporation employs, as of the present time, some 6,463 persons. They have an annual payroll of $23,857,000. Through this operation they produce on the average about 58,000 passenger cars and 13,000 trucks which is a total of about 71,000 motor vehicles altogether per annum. If you figure this out I think you will come to the conclusion that there are
The Address-Mr. D. F. Brown nearly 300 motor vehicles produced every working day of the year by that plant alone.
This is not just for the benefit of one locality or one corporation, for the expenditure which is made by that corporation is spread over the whole of Canada from British Columbia to Nova Scotia and Newfoundland. All of us benefit by the materials which are purchased and the sales which are made to the various dealers.
These companies sell through dealers and these dealers give a warranty backed up by the company. That warranty is for the good workmanship of the car and is for the period of the first 90 days or the first 4,000 miles driven by the purchaser or whichever occurs first. That, Mr. Speaker, is the practice not of one company only; it is the practice of all the companies.
I am sorry that the hon. member for Hastings-Frontenac (Mr. White) is not present in his seat, although I have notified his office that I was going to bring this matter up tonight.* However, I may say that he and I are the very best of friends, and as a member of the opposition he is, I can safely say, probably one of my closest friends and severest critics. But Mr. Speaker, I abhor the practice of using this forum of the House of Commons for the purpose of airing personal grievances, and I do so for these reasons. First, that it is an abuse of our regularly constituted courts in this country which are set up for the purpose of providing redress for any wrong that may be suffered.
Second, it is a wanton waste of taxpayers' money to air these grievances here at such expense to the people of Canada on what is a purely personal matter.
Third, it precludes the person charged from defending himself in a fair and honest manner. He is not permitted to come to this house for the purpose of giving his evidence, defending himself and taking his own chances.
Finally, Mr. Speaker, it is my opinion that such practice, if adhered to, will result in a form of legal blackmail.
As I said before, I would like to refer to the remarks made by the hon. member for Hastings-Frontenac during the course of this debate which may be found on page 86 of Hansard dated November 17, 1953, and on page 87, where you will find he says:
In a recent matter that came through my law office I was amazed to find that the great Chrysler Corporation of Canada, which manufactures Chrysler, De Soto, Dodge and Plymouth cars, makes no warranty in the sale of their cars.
As I have said, I have no brief for any corporation, but I do hold a brief for the people of my constituency, and for the workers in the factories, for in addition to
*(See page 195.)

The Address-Mr. D. F. Brown all the large automobile factories we have some 50-odd feeder plants which supply parts and materials to these manufacturing agencies, and these people have a great pride in their workmanship. They have a great love of their work and they take great satisfaction in having accomplished a good job.
In my opinion, Mr. Speaker, while not intended to be so, it is a rebuff to say the least to the little people of my constituency who are charged with having performed a bad job.
I continue to quote from his speech. He says:
In fact, under the terms of the purchase, any such representation or warranty is specifically excluded.
And he continues further on-I want to quote him fairly:
But the Chrysler corporation made it very plain to me that no such warranty exists, and if someone is unlucky or unfortunate enough to purchase one of their cars which is defective, a car that is a "lemon", he is simply out of luck as far as the corporation is concerned.
And further down he says:
It appeared that everything that could possibly be wrong was wrong with the car.
Now, I do not deny for one moment that my friend, the hon. member for Hastings-Frontenac, had some complaint about the car. But let us see what his complaint is and how it was handled. I find later on in his speech he says this:
It would appear that an important company such as Chrysler, having turned out a lemon of a car like this, would at least replace it with a new car in proper shape.
This is the crucial part of his speech. I think that is most effective. This is a report, as he puts it, of a client of the hon. member.
Well now, I am not going to say that that old legal maxim is correct, that he who acts as his own solicitor ... I will not say that because it will not apply, but I had a search made in the offices of the company concerned and they could find no record of any such client of my hon. friend having made any complaint. But they did find that my hon. friend made a complaint so that he is the client referred to in his speech.
I have with me correspondence on this matter and I would like to review it for members of this house. This is correspondence which was had with my hon. friend and I again regret that he is not here.

I do not know what they mean by "a few hundred miles" but I suppose it might be 300, or it might be 500-or, to be generous, let us say it is 800 miles.

I thought that, as a member of this house, I should have the best information available about two things: the development of the port of Churchill-a resolution on the order paper will give me a chance to say something about that a little later on-and the present and future needs of our best customer. I discussed this question and presumed that those to whom I spoke were in the position that most civil servants are in some time or another when they give to governments advice which they think is good. Sometimes that advice is taken and sometimes it is not. After the decision is made they make the very best possible case that can be made for the situation. However, the people I saw at the British ministry of food were anxious to have the people of Canada appreciate the fact that Great Britain will never forget our contribution in food during the war and since the war. They have very much appreciated the quality and quantity of Canadian food which has come to the United Kingdom. They would like to have British Columbia apples, Nova Scotia apples, Canadian cheese, meats, eggs, pork and salmon, but the dollar crisis forces them to decide how many dollars can be spent in Canada and what they will buy with those dollars. Canadian wheat is the best wheat sold in the world. It makes the best bread. The British people are anxious to have as much Canadian wheat as they can for as long as they can. They explained what really is and has been as simple as A,B,C. Unless ways and means can be found to get an increasing volume of British goods into our market it is only going to be a matter of time until their purchases of Canadian wheat will decrease-particularly if there are other wheat producing countries in the world which are going to be prepared to take British manufactured goods. It is a problem that all members of all political parties are going to have to face up to very quickly. I would like to suggest that careful consideration be given to the proposals suggested by the leader of this group on Monday when he advocated that we should:
(a)	accept sterling as a means of part payment for some of our wheat and other agricultural surpluses, including commodities such as salmon and apples, which those countries have got from us in large quantities in the past.
(b)	. . . place a higher proportion of our foreign orders for governmental supplies in the sterling area. . . .

(c). . . lower tariffs and dumping duties on their exports to us; and, (d) we suggest too as an emergency measure, the postponement of further capital and interest payments on the United Kingdom loan obtained from us in 1946, which was to run for a period of 3J years.
I might suggest one additional point and it is that an import board should be established. I know that the present government has not had a mandate to set up an import board, but I remind you that it did not have a mandate from the people to set up a crown corporation to buy silk, rubber and sugar during the war years. However, if the government had not used foresight and anticipated requirements during the war the Canadian war effort could have been quite different.
I suggest an import board that would accept in the sterling area commodities that might come to Canada which could and would be fed into the regular channels of trade through wholesalers and retailers in our country without disrupting present established manufacturing, wholesaling and retailing industries. By means of an import board we could increase the volume of British imports. So I suggest that the government give consideration to this point coming from this corner of the house with a view to solving the complex international trade problems that affect not only the farmers but everyone in the Dominion of Canada.
While I was in London I met one of our former colleagues, Colonel Alan Chambers, D.S.O., who came here from Nanaimo in 1940 when I came. He suggested that before returning to Canada I should pay a visit to Vimy and the world war I memorials in France. This seemed quite a good suggestion. I had not been to the continent since 1926 and I welcomed this chance to go over there. Some time again I want to take a little bit more time to discuss Vimy particularly. The visit to Vimy is one that one will never forget. We saw it in the moonlight one beautiful night. I had forgotten that on that memorial there are the names of 11,285 of our fellow Canadians whose graves were not found in France in 1914-18. I was only 13 years of age when the first war broke out. I remember that among the first boys who left from our home town in Ontario was one of my boyhood heroes. He was one of the best ballplayers I had ever seen at that time of life. I was a country boy. He called me by name. I never forgot that. I had forgotten that my young friend was only 22 years of age when he lost his life in France. I found his name on the

Vimy memorial. On one of the other memorials nearby I found this inscription:
Here are recorded the names of the 73,307 officers and men of the British armies who fell in the Somme battlefields, July 1915 to February 1918, but to whom the fortunes of war denied the known and honoured burial given to their comrades in death.
In still another cemetery I found these words:
That the world may remember two and one-half million dead here have been laid side by side soldiers of France and the British empire in eternal comradeship.
At Dieppe, of course, we saw the graves of many gallant young Canadians who lost their lives in the second world war.
I was reminded of my visit to Europe in 1926 when I was a student at university, when young people were greatly concerned about fitting into a society that seemed to have so few openings. The European countries particularly found in a few short years that a serious unemployment problem had developed. Most of the young people were concerned about getting into business or the various professions. I recall that when the suggestion was made of going into politics and trying to do something about the complex international problems that prevailed, they dismissed very lightly the thought of entering the political field. Politics was a business for the aged but not for the young. During the years between world war I and world war II we did not expend sufficient effort in trying to solve our international problems.
After this visit to the continent I paid a brief visit to the United Nations headquarters in New York. I think I am saying what delegates from many countries believe, namely that Canada enjoys an enviable reputation in the United Nations. Our own Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Pearson) did credit to himself and to our country during the year that he was president. I was there as a visitor so I believe I can say that our delegates, advisers and staff at the United Nations clearly have the confidence and the esteem of people from a great many countries. However, I do not think that we have done our maximum. We are strategically situated, with a long connection with the United Kingdom and wedged in between two powerful nations, the United States and the U.S.S.R.

It would, I think, be a mistake to assume that nothing can be settled with Soviet Russia unless or until everything is settled. A settlement of two or three of our difficulties would be an important gain to every peace-loving country ... It certainly would do no harm if, for a while, each side looked about for things to do which would be agreeable instead of being disagreeable to each other . . .
We all desire that the Russian people should take the high place in world affairs which is their due without feeling anxiety about their own security. I do not believe that the immense problem of reconciling the security of Russia with the freedom and safety of western Europe is insoluble. Indeed, if the United Nations Organization had the authority and character for which its creators hoped, it would be solved already.
Then he referred to a telegram which he sent to Stalin in 1945, on April 29. Here is the telegram:
There is not much comfort in looking into a future where you and the countries you dominate, plus the communist parties in many other states, are all drawn up on one side, and those who rally to the English-speaking nations and their associates or dominions are on the other. It is quite obvious that their quarrel would tear the world to pieces, and that all of us leading men on either side who had anything to do with that would be shamed before history. Even embarking on a long period of suspicions, of abuse and counter-abuse, and of opposing policies would be a disaster hampering the great developments of world prosperity for the masses which are attainable only by our trinity.
Then he suggested the hope for an early conference. He said:
I must make it plain that, in spite of all the uncertainties and confusion in which world affairs are plunged, I believe that a conference on the highest level should take place between the leading powers without long delay. This conference should not be overhung by a ponderous or rigid agenda, or led into mazes and jungles of technical details, zealously contested by hordes of experts and officials drawn up in vast, cumbrous array ... It might well be that no hard-faced agreements would be reached, but there might be a general feeling among those gathered together that they might do something better than tear the human race, including themselves, into bits.
For instance, they might be attracted, as President Eisenhower has shown himself to be, and as Pravda does not challenge, by the idea of letting the weary, toiling masses of mankind enter upon the best spell of good fortune, fair play, well-being, leisure and harmless happiness that has ever been within their reach or even within their dreams.
I only say that this might happen, and I do not see why anyone should be frightened at having a try for it. If there is not at the summit of the nations the will to win the greatest prize and the greatest honour ever offered to mankind, doomladen responsibility will fall upon those who now possess the power to decide. At the worst the participants in the meeting would have established more intimate contacts. At the best we might have a generation of peace.

The Address-Mr. Nicholson
I have taken some time to read rather extensively from that speech but I think it is a speech that more Canadians should read.
I want to make a suggestion to the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent), who is embarking on a world-wide tour after the Christmas vacation-and he is to be commended for his imagination in making this good will tour. My suggestion is that he include Moscow in his tour. I do not make this suggestion facetiously. The Prime Minister, I think, would not be suspected, even by McCarthy, of having any subversive leanings. I think the Prime Minister of Canada might well have said, as did Mr. Churchill, that it would certainly do no harm if for a while each side looked about for things to do which would be agreeable instead of being disagreeable to the other. I would suggest that if the Prime Minister did include a brief stay in Moscow in his tour it would certainly do no harm and it might do a great deal of good.
As I have indicated before, I think that Canada has a very important role in the present critical international situation and I would like to suggest more active support for three of the specialized agencies that are pretty vital to us. They are FAO, WHO and UNESCO. With the very large supply of food we have on hand and cannot use, I think it should be recognized that food would be a very powerful weapon for good will which would help counteract the communist influences that are very active all over the world.
It is obvious that western farmers and the cheese producers of Ontario are not in a position to make large gifts, but I would suggest that since we are spending $2,000 million for defence each year we should take a larger percentage of that than we are taking to feed hungry people when the food would make such a difference.
I would like to refer to a job that a very distinguished Canadian is doing. He is Dr. Keenleyside, who is director of technical assistance for the United Nations. Dr. Keenleyside was the guest speaker for the Canadian Federation of Agriculture convention which took place at Victoria last winter. He gave us some information that we should have a look at. He said:
Over half the people of the world are ill, though most of them could be cured and many of the most prevalent diseases could be permanently eradicated. Those of you who were bom in Canada can expect to live, on the average, 70 years -the biblical three score and ten. Women of course average an extra two years. . . But in over 20 countries, including some of the largest in the world, the life expectancy even for women is about 30 years.
The leader of this party mentioned last night that two people out of three in the


world go hungry. Two out of every three never get enough to eat, though I imagine in Canada more Canadians suffer from eating too much rather than too little. Half the adults in the world cannot read or write. Perhaps 100 years ago we could argue that it really did not concern us how people lived in Africa or Asia or anywhere else. The important place was Ottawa. But the world has grown so small that if there is poverty, if there is disease, if there is ignorance in one part of the world, it should concern us. With the airplane, television and the radio, our neighbours all over the world know the very high standard that we enjoy while they live in poverty.
Dr. Keenleyside says:
Most of the people in the world cannot afford decent clothing, housing and recreation. Even in Canada the average income per capita is just over $1,000 per year . . .
That means $1,000 for every man, woman and child, and though we probably do not all get our share, that is the average. But two-thirds of the people in the world have an average income of $100 a year.
Mr. Speaker, if two-thirds of the people of the world have to live on $100 a year while we are living on $1,000 a year, it looks to me as though there is trouble ahead.
Dr. Keenleyside concludes, and here I shall also conclude my remarks:
It is at this point that I believe our present Canadian policy to be gravely inadequate. It seems to me to be unreasonable to devote $100 to direct military defence for every $1 we give to the saving of the underdeveloped areas of the world. Although Canada does more than most countries, our annual contribution to the T. A. programs of the United Nations is about equal to the cost of one bomber. Even adding the amount we are providing under the Colombo plan the total is still just about what we spend on a single destroyer.
By strengthening the still free but dangerously unstable parts of the world we are strengthening our own defences. Dollars spent on technical and financial assistance may eventually mean dollars saved on bombs. Every teacher or doctor or engineer or economist or agricultural expert sent out today will reduce the likelihood of our having to send sailors, soldiers and airmen tomorrow. I suggest that it is better to send Canadians with seeds and test-tubes and slide rules to help build better farms and hospitals and factories, than to send million-dollar aircraft to drop atom bombs on enemy cities. Admittedly we cannot be sure that we can avoid the one by doing the other. But if we don't assist the nations that need help we certainly make it more likely that we shall have to fight.

Mr. Speaker, may I avail myself of this opportunity to offer my congratulations on your election to the high office that you now bold. Your duties, in directing the business of the

house, are very important, and I am sure you will discharge them to the satisfaction of every hon. member.
May I also congratulate the mover (Mr. Hollingworth) and the seconder (Mr. Ville-neuve) of the address. They have fulfilled very well a rather difficult task, even though we have a good government in the country, and I congratulate them for having had the courage and initiative that a young member must have to break the ice at the beginning of a new session. It is always difficult for a young member to make his maiden speech. The expression "break the ice" is quite appropriate, because the atmosphere in the House of Commons, as well as the atmosphere in the legislatures of our Canadian provinces, is rather cold when compared to the atmosphere on the hustings. I congratulate them because they have fulfilled their task to everyone's satisfaction. They have shown that they have what it takes and I am confident that they will make a very important contribution to the work of the house. That is why I also wish to extend my congratulations to the people of their respective constituencies for having elected them at the last election.
May I also, Mr. Speaker, greet the two new ministers: the Secretary of State (Mr. Pickersgill), new member from Newfoundland, and the hon. member for Montmagny-L'lslet (Mr. Lesage), who has always been my good friend. Being men of talent, initiative and eager for work, they will make a worth-while contribution to the debates of the house and they will give the necessary assistance to the government so that they may fulfil the task the people expect from them.
I have listened very closely to the various speeches made since the beginning of the session. I read several times the speech of the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Drew) after listening to it, and I would like, Mr. Speaker, to say a few words about it to the house. At page 34 of this session's Hansard, we find the following, from the mouth, the very lips of the leader of the Conservative opposition:
No matter what differences of opinion we may have as to the way in which the business of this country can best be conducted, and it will be a good thing for Canada if those differences are always expressed in firm and vigorous terms, there is, I am sure, agreement throughout the house that the Prime Minister has and will occupy that high office with distinction and in a manner entirely in keeping with Canada's high position among the nations of the world. I most sincerely extend to him my personal good wishes for health and happiness as he carries out his great responsibilities, responsibilities associated with the whole conduct of this house and of the nation.
The Address-Mr. P. Gauthier
It is very stimulating, Mr. Speaker, to hear the leader of an opposing party address those words to our Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent). This is surely the proper spirit to show at all times in the discussions and the debates both of this house and of our legislative assemblies.
Mr. Speaker, the hon. Leader of the Opposition added these well-chosen words:
At a time when there is so much bitterness and strife throughout the world, it is a happy incident of our life in this country that, while we hold firm convictions along party lines, friendships are formed between the members of the parliament of Canada which are in no way limited by the affiliations through which we seek to serve our constituents and our country.
Mr. Speaker, I was reminded there of a late member of this house, the former member for Peel, Mr. Gordon Graydon. 1 had first met Mr. Graydon in January, 1936, which means that his demise has been a true loss to me. I knew the member for Peel very well. For eighteen years we sat in this house together. Moreover we were both members of the committee on external affairs where, most of the time, I was of one mind with him on certain problems facing the Canadian government and the Canadian people as well as the rest of the world.
The former member for Peel was a man who served his country for the pleasure and the satisfaction he derived from it, a man who always put spiritual values far above material values, and that was the source of his strength and what compelled a greater admiration on our part. Gordon Graydon always contemplated great things for his country, and I have no doubt that the years he spent in the House of Commons have been very useful not only to his party but for the whole of Canada.
Mr. Speaker, during these last few years the federal government has enacted measures which parliament has ratified. It has passed an act for the conservation of waste lands, the reforestation of those waste lands and of our timber lands, a part of which is destroyed each year either through disease or through fire. I have always been in favour of such measures. I have even risen in this house to better support those measures, but I have always regretted that the Quebec provincial government, the government of my province, did not deem advisable to accept the help offered by the federal government in enacting such measures designed to help the provinces with their forests.
I see, for example, that the province of Ontario, during the fiscal year 1952-53, received $214,000 for the inventory of its forests. It has spent $187,830 of this federal grant.

As far as reforestation goes, the federal government spent $75,000 while the province of Ontario spent $71,206. On the other hand, when I glance at Quebec's column, I see nothing there but an empty space. Needless to say how really sorry I am that no agreement was reached between the government of my province and the federal government; had such an agreement been signed, our provincial government could have helped all those who, directly or indirectly, are interested in the conservation of our forests and who do all they possibly can, drawing on their knowledge or on their financial means, in order to protect as far as possible, the estates they rent or have in freehold.
One cannot reasonably pretend, Mr. Speaker, that the autonomy of the province of Quebec would be violated by an agreement between the two governments. I do not see in what way that autonomy would be violated and I can see it all the less now that I have read the two bills adopted in 1949; it seems to me that whatever amount of good will is displayed by the provincial government, however sound their policy may be, the federal government could still provide help which would certainly be of some advantage.
It might interest you to read a book written by a highly qualified forestry engineer, whose proficiency is the result of his deep knowledge and of his vast experience. If you read this book, "Land of Milk and Honey" or "Wilderness of Cain", by Mr. Thomas Maher, you would soon see that my province does not only require the intelligent and concrete policy I spoke about a moment ago, but that it also needs the assistance of all men and governments of good will.

the Treasury in the United States. These words, mind you, were uttered after our election on August 10, 1953.

speechtext: Who is he?

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Secretary of the Treasury in the United States. He is somebody! What I am about to read is reported in the U.S News and World Report. At a conference of the national press club on September 16, 1953, a question was put to Mr. Humphrey, probably by a journalist, in these words:
How is it Canada can cut taxes and still have a higher dollar income on tax collection? If this is possible in Canada, why would not the result be the same in the United States?
Mr. Humphrey's answer was this:
I am glad you ask about Canada, because before I became a bureaucrat I was up there a good deal and spending a lot of money there. I think Canada has been a little smarter than we have been. I think they have run their country a little better than we have. I think they have had a little sounder fundamental condition, and they have had them right straight along over a period of the last several years, not just a few but ten or fifteen.
I might remind the house, sir, that during those ten or fifteen years it was the Liberal government that was in power at the time and they were doing their job very successfully in governing Canada. I continue with the answer of Mr. Humphrey:
They have been making great progress. Canada is in a period of very definite development. It has tremendous natural resources. I won't try to sell it to you, although I am a great bull on Canada. I think they have great future prospects. They are a little ahead of us, and have been a little ahead of us right along.
I wanted to give those words to my hon. friends so that they will keep in mind the fact that the future of Canada is still great.
(Translation) :
Mr. Speaker, during the last general election-and I intend neither to analyse all the principal phases of the general election that has just taken place nor to revive the various discussions that were held in my county- one of the subjects which was discussed, not very often yet often enough, is the question of the Family Allowances Act. I wish to submit to the house a few notes I took during a lecture by an employee of the family allowances district office in Quebec. I want to tell the house as well as the members and all the people about it, for a great part of our public may not know about the social and humanitarian aspects of family allowances. The Quebec members, and the general public too, may not know to what extent the Family Allowances Act has been a happy complement

The Address-Mr. P. Gauthier
to the compulsory school attendance act which was passed by Quebec under the inspiration of another Liberal government, that of Mr. Godbout, during the time he was in power, from 1939 to 1944. Mr. Speaker, allow me to show you how family allowances have contributed to extend for two years longer the compulsory school attendance act in the province of Quebec. The house will see no objection, I hope, if I rely on the notes I have now in front of me. I said that this act that we have in the province of Quebec is well thought of by the whole population and all classes of society. This act would become ineffective if its practical application were ignored. I hope it is complied with, both by the government itself and by its officials. It would serve no purpose to build a beautiful large school and have a compulsory school attendance act if the latter were not complied with. This act provides that children must attend school until the age of 14. The attendance is checked by those whom we call attendance supervisors. They are not policemen, of course, but almost voluntary supervisors, so to speak, whose function it is to see that this act is complied with, as well as to convince parents and children that it is a duty for them to observe the law. Therefore they should not see in this supervisor a policeman, but a man who fulfils his duty. I hope that act is observed and I might say, welcomed, by all classes of
society and all faiths in my province. I hope that the act, properly enforced, will allow all the children of the province of Quebec to attend school and get at least the minimum of education necessary today. Evidently, that legislation marks real progress for our educational system and that is why I earnestly urge our people to observe it as they should. The task of an attendance supervisor is somewhat like that of a social worker. As I said a moment ago, these attendance supervisors, through persuasion and understanding and kind words, may help children and parents alike understand that that measure is bound to produce happy results.
I was saying, Mr. Speaker, that our people are not sufficiently aware of the social and humanitarian consequences of the Family Allowances Act. That is why I wanted to say how this Family Allowances Act which, although it was not originally accepted throughout the provinces, is, I believe, readily subscribed to now, has helped to further education in our province. Because of it mothers and fathers have once more convinced themselves that they can now count on a really appreciable amount every month with which to send their children to school, with which to dress them better so that when they appear in public it is now impossible to distinguish to which class of society they belong.
